newsitem.title: UK: Diana finds you just can't keep the staff.
newsitem.headline: Diana finds you just can't keep the staff.

text.p: Sylvia McDermott, who on Wednesday reached a settlement in an unfair dismissal claim against Britain's Princess Diana, is the latest in a long line of staff to have had a showdown with their royal boss.
Like any large household headed by a high-profile family, Diana relies on an array of support staff ranging from secretaries and nannies to bodyguards, drivers and PR consultants.
Over the past 16 years many have departed from her palace, although few have succeeded in making their grievances known.
Some, like former housekeeper Wendy Berry, have tried to capitalise on their privileged access to the world's most talked-about princess by writing books or selling photographs to the tabloid press.

Diana has abandoned traditional royal reticence in going to the courts to silence them, but this time it was she who risked being summoned to explain herself in public, although she did not in the end have to appear.

At an industrial tribunal on Wednesday, lawyers for the princess and McDermott announced an out-of-court settlement under which the former maid receives an undisclosed cash sum. She also remains bound by a confidentialty clause from publishing anything about her time in the royal household.
Top of the high-profile staff to have fallen out with Diana were her press secretary Geoff Crawford and her public relations consultant Jane Atkinson.

Crawford resigned in 1995 over Diana's dramatic decision to give an in-depth television interview about her failed marriage, her infidelity and her wish to be a "Queen of people's hearts". The princess had failed to warn him in advance about the interview.
Atkinson resigned abruptly last August after just six months in the job following rumours that the two had clashed over how to manage Diana's image after her divorce.

The palace exodus started soon after Diana's 1981 marriage to heir to the throne Prince Charles when she made clear her husband's long serving personal valet Stephen Barry, who was gay, was no longer wanted.
Nanny Barbara Barnes left in 1987 after five years service amid reports that Diana resented her close relationship with sons William and Harry.
A year later another nanny, Lizzie Spring, lasted only a day after reportedly reciting a Tennyson poem to William instead of reading him a children's book.
One recently-compiled newspaper list named 32 people who had either been ousted or resigned from Diana's staff in the past 15 years.
The latest was personal aide Victoria Mendham, who quit in January after seven years following a disagreement with what she called her "demanding boss".
Diana has several times taken swift legal action against those who have betrayed her trust but has never been in the dock herself.

Britain's industrial tribunal system is less formal than the civil or criminal courts but has the power to cross-examine witnesses and award fines and compensation, usually in relation to dismissal from jobs or the treatment of employees in the workplace.
Last week Diana reached an out of court settlement for libel with the Daily Express newspaper over its claim that she would benefit financially from the planned charity auction of her ballgowns.

In 1994, she was prepared to become the first member of the royal family this century to testify in open court when she sued the Daily Mirror for publishing sneak photographs of her exercising in a London gym. The breach of confidence case was also ended in an out of court settlement.
